location_standardised: New Zealand
brief_context: The nation whose electrical development is the main subject.
brief_extract:
Statistics show that this Dominion uses more domestic
electricity per head of the population than any other
country in the world. The explanation is that New Zealand, mountainous
and overrun by great rivers and lakes, whose overflow
tumbles furiously through narrow gorges to the sea,
makes her electricity from cheap water-power. Like
Russia, Scandinavia and certain parts of the United
States of America, this Dominion has built gigantic dams
across rivers and lake outlets, which she has equipped
with dynamos and large storage units; then she has sat
back to enjoy a constant and cheap supply of power.

location_standardised: London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Mentioned as a landmark near the new University building.

article_title: THE PLACE OF ELECTRICITY IN A FITTER BRITAIN
brief_extract: Even now, when to describe the use of electricity as universal would be far from the truth, this smoke pall is lifting; the centralised and scientifically-regulated burning of coal in the great power stations is having its effect, and if this scheme is carried still further it will no doubt clear the air of our great cities even more; fewer citizens will breathe impure air and be shut in by a blanket of fog in the future. Nor are the giant power stations as ugly as their essential modernity might suggest; the twin chimneys of Battersea power station, with their white plumes of smoke, are far less offensive to my eyes than, say, the hotch-potch of factories derelict in appearance which stand along London's noble river reaches. Electricity would have performed a priceless service to the town-dweller if it had only got rid of the lowering clouds over his city; it has, however, achieved more good deeds.

location_standardised: Enfield, Middlesex, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Location of Belling's Works visited by members.
brief_extract:
During the year five Tea-talks have been arranged, the subjects being: "The Story of the Herring Industry"; "Varied Breakfast and Supper Dishes"; "Sunshine and Health"; "Summer Dishes and Cooling Drinks"; and "St. Dunstan's and its Work."
Members have visited Belling's Works at Enfield, where cookers and fires can be seen in course of manufacture; Gillett's Works at Isleworth, where razors and razor-blades are made in millions; Watney Combe's Brewery at Mortlake, where electric cooperage and electrical machinery used in brewing is to be seen; and Maclean's Chemical Laboratory at Brentford, where many chemical products are prepared. A party of 96 members and friends took part in the evening trip round London during Coronation time to view the flood-lit buildings and decorations.

brief_context: Site of the 1938 E.A.W. Annual Conference.
brief_extract:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE. SPRING, 1938

EDITORIAL

THE 1938 Annual Conference of the Electrical Association for Women is due to take place in London from April 27th to 29th at the Park Lane Hotel, and although the Association is organising yet another Conference this summer to be held in Glasgow in connection with the Empire Exhibition and described elsewhere in this magazine, the numbers for the annual convention are by no means diminished, and promise as successful an occasion as ever. Apart from the obvious necessity for a common meeting ground for any large organisation such as our own, the pleasures of meeting new people, of again seeing old friends from other parts of the country, the opportunities for interchange of ideas and points of view, all these are things that any intelligent person welcomes.

location_standardised: Scotland, United Kingdom
brief_context: Location of Special Areas for nutrition work.
brief_extract:
"In view of the nation-wide interest in Nutrition and Physical Fitness, allied as these are to a fuller enjoyment of life for the whole community, this National Conference of The Electrical Association for Women resolves:—
That greater facilities should be provided everywhere for acquiring a knowledge of cooking, economic buying and household management. That fuller publicity should be given to the facts regarding the nutritive values of food ordinarily in use, and
That electrical housecraft classes should be established at all domestic science centres."
A practical example of what can be done towards these ends is the appointment of Miss Mary Mackirdy, of Glasgow, as Adviser in Cookery and Nutrition to Women's Community Service or Unemployed Clubs in the Special Areas in Scotland. Miss Mackirdy's work consists of organising the cookery activities in the clubs described, advising on cookery equipment, taking personally a series of demonstrations of simple and nutritious dishes, preceded by a general talk on food values, and finding voluntary instructors in cookery to assist or to continue her own work.

brief_extract: In the Mobile Vans there are enormous drums to carry this cable, for when doing television Outside Broadcasts the camera has frequently to travel long distances from the transmitting van, as for instance when touring a film studio. brief_context: Highland village buildings constructed from plaster casts from here.
brief_extract:
The Highland village—or an Clachan, as they say in
Gaelic—shows the real old Scotland, the Scotland that
is fast passing before the relentless march of modernity. A laird’s castle, a smithy, an inn, a pre-Reformation
kirk, a post office and several cottages comprise the
village, which has been constructed from full-size plaster
casts of existing buildings in Argyll, Skye and the Outer
Isles. In the laird’s castle there is a hall where ceilidhs
are held, and here the visitor will hear the plaintive
melodies of the Hebrides sung as only the Islesmen can
sing them.

Some cattle
are kept for immediate necessities,
there are plenty of horses for the
guests to ride, and a proper comple-

in the large hats, bright scarves and
fancy shirts and boots which are
well known to film-goers. These
boys, generally called Tex and
Hank and Pud, as they should be,
are wonderful horsemen, and also
very knowledgeable about their coun-
try, about the beasts, birds and
plants of the Arizona deserts which
contain much that is unusual, and
have not been very thoroughly
explored, even yet, by naturalists. The cowboys look after the horses,
allot you your mount, after a swift

and quite silent glance at you by
which they gauge your probable
capacities in the saddle, and take
the guests out in large riding parties,
to see that they don't fall off.

Cardinal - birds with their
magenta-scarlet plumage came to
bird-tables around the ranch; there

cactus-wrens, horned wrens, two

a Ford truck a very vulgar, undigni-

tudes. Coyotes howled close to

The Courtyard, with the Banqueting Hall to the right of the Tower. DARTINGTON HALL

THE ease with which electrical power can be transported and distributed has made it no longer necessary for industry to be centred round the coal mines, and the internal combustion engine, with the consequent development of road transport, has removed the other obstacle to decentralisation, so there is no reason why other industries than agriculture should not flourish in the country. To begin
with, the tenant of the home farm was persuaded to
stay on as a salaried manager and his farmstead re-
designed and equipped. Repairing the old buildings and
restoring the garden and grounds took six years, and
when it was finished the skilled men who had carried
it out became the personnel of three departments,

and the Gardens Department. While the work of restoration was proceeding other
departments were formed: another dairy farm was
started on different lines to the home farm; the
orchards were taken over by a department, which
also made cider and grew vegetables; the woods were
taken over by the Woodlands Department, and a
further 1,200 acres were bought to make an economic
unit for management; a sawmill was built to deal
with the timber; a textile mill was built to restore
one of the native industries; and, in addition, a poultry
farm, a sheep farm and a pig farm were started.

location_standardised: London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Theatre rebuilt by Lilian Baylis for opera and ballet.
brief_extract: It took a long time to get good regular audiences but by various means, such as persuading important people to talk about Shakespeare before the curtain in the intervals of opera, and even more, one suspects, through the undeniable enthusiasm of Miss Baylis and the band of young voluntary helpers who had rallied round her, the enterprise grew to the proportions it has reached to-day. In the meantime Miss Baylis had borrowed money and rebuilt the historic Sadlers Wells Theatre in North London, intending to present alternate performances of opera, ballet and Shakespeare in the two theatres. It was quickly discovered, however, that the cost of carting scenery and properties to and fro would more than swallow the profits, and so Sadlers Wells is devoted to such performances of opera and ballet as challenge comparison with more haughty rivals in the centre of London, while Shakespeare and classical plays are given at the Old Vic, to which one suspects that even hardened dramatic critics go with a stirring of expectation.

brief_extract:
HOME WORKERS' CAMPAIGN
The generosity of Sir John and Lady Snell has been the beginning of a Bursary Fund to be used for the formation of Home Workers' Classes in the Special Areas. This donation is the practical outcome of Lady Snell's suggestion to the Council that Branches in the more prosperous areas should help those who are less well off to institute courses, a suggestion which has already been followed up by the Sutton Coldfield Branch. The organisation of Home Workers' Classes continues to develop, and Branches have found that new members are being attracted to the Association through these courses, which offer the practical information on domestic electricity that many women seek.

Beauchamp, late Commercial Manager of the Central Elec-

country visited the British Industries Fair at Birmingham in

Management. The Teachers' Circle programme consisted largely of joint
meetings with the Demonstrators, as these are proving in-
creasingly helpful to both groups.

The Queen's Message
WHEN within three months an Association organises no less than four conferences, two national and two for area federations, at which the total attendance amounts to some seventeen hundred, it shows a phenomenal enthusiasm among the members—enthusiasm borne of conviction in the purposes of the Association. The second national conference arranged by the Electrical Association for Women this Summer was held at the Empire Exhibition, Glasgow, on the theme "The New Way of Living—Women's Work in the Modern World." To the President of the E.A.W., Her Majesty the Queen, supporter of all progressive work, graciously sent this message:
WINDSOR CASTLE

article_title: TIME, TIME KEEPING AND CLOCKS Part 2
brief_extract: It is tempting to linger over some of the by-ways of watchmaking—the fat old verge watches known irreverently as “turnips”; the beautiful early English levers; the mechanism of wonderful calendar watches which not only showed the day of the week, the date, and phases of the moon, but actually allowed for the disturbance of Leap Year; of repeaters that tell the time to the nearest minute by their charming bell-like tone; and of many other delightful things. The temptation must be resisted, for electricity, like the younger generation, is “knocking at the door.” But one suggestion may be made to any reader who cares for these matters: that a visit should be paid to the Science Museum at South Kensington, where some magnificent old clocks can be seen working, also to the Guildhall collection of watches. The instant response of electricity, its speed in action, and its convenience, were bound sooner or later to be applied to the measurement of time.

article_title: THE NEW WAY OF LIVING: WOMEN’S WORK IN THE MODERN WORLD
brief_extract: The dignity and colour, and at the same time the friendly atmosphere of this inaugural function boded well for the success of the Conference as a whole, an augury which the succeeding days were amply to fulfil. The formal sessions of the Conference, entitled “The New Way of Living: Women’s Work in the Modern World,” were held at the Empire Exhibition in the Fashion Theatre of the Women of Empire Pavilion, and here, before a crowded and attentive audience, our President opened the proceedings on Monday morning by reading Her Majesty’s gracious message. In her subsequent remarks, Lady Swaythling reminded us that the Queen’s interest in the aims and work of the Association were the more natural in view of the fact that she made her first public speech as Duchess of York at the now historic Wembley Conference of 1924, of which to-day’s great gathering was but the logical sequel.

An old person requires less food per day
than a young one. People living in cold climates require
more heat forming foods than those living in hot
climates, that is why Esquimaux have a liking for tallow
candles as a diet and require about ten pounds of whale-

Crab Royal

3 tablespoons butter
3 tablespoons flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/4 teaspoon paprika
1 egg, slightly beaten
2/3 cup milk
2/3 cup chicken stock
1 cup flaked cooked crabmeat
1/2 cup sliced, cooked mushrooms

article_title: The English E.A.W. visit the Dutch E.A.W.
brief_extract:
It was a calm passage
and we came up the Maas in brilliant
sunshine on Thursday morning, eagerly
watching the surrounding country. A tour of Rotterdam was arranged for
the afternoon, and we set out to see this
interesting city with its numerous water-
ways and fine buildings. A visit was
made to the Electricity Department.

brief_extract:
We numbered
43, and amongst us was the Lady
Mayoress of Hull, who is a member of
the Hull Branch. It was a calm passage
and we came up the Maas in brilliant
sunshine on Thursday morning, eagerly
watching the surrounding country. A tour of Rotterdam was arranged for

interesting city with its numerous water-
ways and fine buildings.

location_standardised: Arnhem, Gelderland, Netherlands
brief_context: City visited by the party by train.
article_title: The English E.A.W. visit the Dutch E.A.W.
brief_extract:
Then followed an-
other drive through Rotterdam, by the
same old windmill on the quay which
saw the departure of the Pilgrim Fathers
to New Amsterdam, and on to the Guild-
hall—a very fine building. The next morning dawned brilliantly,
and we set off to catch the nine-ten train
to Arnhem. The Dutch are friendly
people, and wherever we went we were
greeted warmly.

location_standardised: Netherlands
brief_context: Country visited by the English E.A.W. party.
article_title: The English E.A.W. visit the Dutch E.A.W.
brief_extract:
Our ship set off for England about
eight o'clock. The sea was like a mill-
pond and we sat on deck watching the
friendly lights of Holland grow dim. We
came up the Humber at noon on Sunday
and were greeted by the strains of the
City Band, and 43 members disembarked
after a farewell to our very kind
Captain.

therie van Weezel; we were all very

visited the celebrated Art Gallery.

THE ELECTRICAL AGE. AUTUMN, 1938

EDITORIAL

“THE domestic revolution might be regarded as the paying by the technicians of a long deferred debt for some of the social consequences of the mechanisation of industry last century.”
This was the keynote of Sir Harold Hartley’s speech when, as Chairman of the International Executive Council and Chairman of the British National Committee, he addressed the Vienna Sectional Meeting of the World Power Conference held from August 25th to September 2nd. In this spirit engineers assembled from the different countries of the world viewed the advent of power in modern life, its past progress and future potentialities.

The wide plateau
with its thousands of acres of sugar cane, banana, pine-
apple, cocoanut and other crops, lies beneath one like,
in a hackneyed but absolutely correct phrase, a giant
chess board. Dotted here and there are little clusters
of low huts, or bungalows, for in many townlets the
only building of any size is the sugar mill; but one
thing you will notice is the absence of any roads, other
than dirt tracks, for the interior of Cuba has no high-
ways worth speaking of except the Central Highway
from Pinar del Rio through Havana to Santiago. This,
stretching for the best part of a thousand miles, was
the work of Machado, the President who was deposed
about five years ago.

contemplating the fine stretches of road which lie

side leading up to lovely houses where fasnionable New

But the rhumba is the real basis of Cuban broad-

birth, the rattle of the maracas and the quick inter-

broadcasting, or to tell you that he himself is hoping
to " go on the air ".

brief_context: Reference to heated tropical houses at the Zoo.
brief_extract:
Langmead

THE availability of modern electrical apparatus in everyday life has considerably improved and extended the interests of the nature-lover, as one well notices when travelling up and down the country. The simplicity and cheapness nowadays of electrical heating devices have enabled the bird-lover to turn the conservatory into a heated aviary for tropical birds, from sugar birds to such gorgeous subjects to be seen at the Zoo’s heated tropical houses, like the toucans, birds-of-paradise and humming birds, according to one’s means. To an even greater extent it has enabled the aquarist to extend his amateur collections to include tropicals in specially heated tanks, so much so that the supplying and introduction of new tropical fish, from angel fish to the gorgeous little Neon tetra of brilliant crimson and emerald green, is a new industry.

location_standardised: London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Mentioned as having zoos with tropical collections and aquaria clubs.
brief_extract: They have enabled the amateur to keep such tropicals as the wasp gobies, the golden tetras, angel fish, fighting fish, black mollies, leopard catfish, harlequins, and many more rare and gorgeous species, for it is not the attraction merely of something new or different which induces the naturalist to keep tropical fish, but the fact that here one may have far more brilliantly-coloured specimens than it is ever possible to dream of in the old-fashioned cold-water aquarium. This is easily seen by a visit to the tropical collections at the Zoos in London, Brighton, Southport (The Arcade, Lord Street), Edinburgh (the Carnegie Aquarium), etc. At London Zoo it has thus been possible to exhibit fish from the coast of Florida, the Red Sea, and Madeira.

The London Branch concluded their Summer Programme with a visit to the Ford Motor Works at Dagenham, where admirers of industrial efficiency toured to their heart's content, and students of the human touch in this machine-made world were able to investigate the remarkable system the Company has evolved for the training of their employees.
